title: Listeria and Nocardia: Two Gram-Positive Rods That Must Not Be Missed
summary: Recognise Listeria monocytogenes (cold growth, room-temperature motility, cephalosporin resistance, neonatal and pregnancy risk) and Nocardia (beaded branching filaments, partial acid-fastness, soil-to-lung-to-brain spread), and separate Nocardia from Actinomyces.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hits 15, 17, 30 and 49 and Trap 6. Listeria facts from Manyi-Loh 2025, Bongiovanni 2024 and Cho 2022 (flagella ≤30 °C, off at 37 °C); Nocardia from Kandi 2015 and Saubolle 2003 (read via a page-fetch tool); Actinomyces from Valour 2014. Not taught as fact (not found in the sources read): the “tumbling” motility pattern, cold enrichment as a lab method, “chalky” colonies, and Actinomyces being non-acid-fast. Saubolle 2003 notes the modified acid-fast stain is less sensitive than the Gram stain, which the reviewer does not mention.

objectives: Describe the key laboratory features and risk groups of Listeria monocytogenes.
Describe the Gram and modified acid-fast appearance, culture needs and clinical spread of Nocardia.
Distinguish Nocardia from Actinomyces and Listeria, and state why cephalosporins do not cover Listeria.

scenes.title: Two gram-positive rods
scenes.altText: Invented scenario, two schematic Gram stains. (1) CSF from a 5-day-old neonate whose mother had a fever before delivery: short gram-positive rods. (2) Sputum from a kidney-transplant recipient on long-term corticosteroids with a lung nodule and new headache: beaded, branching gram-positive filaments. Question token: “Which organism, and what must the lab tell the team?”

cues.text: Two Gram stains. First, cerebrospinal fluid from a five-day-old baby: short gram-positive rods.
Second, sputum from a transplant recipient on steroids, with a lung nodule and a new headache: beaded, branching gram-positive filaments.
Which organisms are these, and what must the lab tell the clinical team?

props.label: Which organism — and what to tell the team?

scenes.title: Listeria monocytogenes
scenes.altText: Profile card: Listeria monocytogenes — gram-positive, non-spore-forming rod; catalase-positive; facultative anaerobe; psychrotrophic (grows from about −0.4 °C to 45 °C, so it multiplies in refrigerated food). Motility card: flagella are produced at or below 30 °C and switched off at 37 °C (MogR repressor and GmaR thermosensor), so motility is shown at room temperature, not at body temperature. Risk card: neonates, pregnant women, the elderly and immunocompromised people; invasive disease includes sepsis, meningitis and rhombencephalitis, and infection in pregnancy can cause miscarriage or stillbirth.

cues.text: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod that forms no spores and is catalase positive. It grows at refrigerator temperatures, so it can multiply in chilled, ready-to-eat food.
It makes flagella at or below thirty degrees and switches them off at thirty-seven. So it is motile at room temperature, not at body temperature.
It mainly harms newborns, pregnant women, older adults and people with weak immunity.
Invasive disease includes sepsis, meningitis and brainstem infection, and infection in pregnancy can cause miscarriage or stillbirth.

scenes.title: Nocardia
scenes.altText: Profile card: Nocardia — aerobic actinomycete; gram-positive, beaded, branching filaments that can fragment; weakly (partially) acid-fast with a modified acid-fast stain using a weak decolouriser (e.g. 1% sulfuric acid); colonies with aerial mycelia, white to orange; usually visible in 2–7 days, slow strains up to 2–3 weeks, so the lab must be told to hold cultures. Ecology card: lives in soil and water; infection by inhalation (pneumonia, abscess, cavities) or through skin; dissemination to brain and other organs, especially with weakened cellular immunity (transplant, corticosteroids, malignancy, AIDS). Stain caveat card: the modified acid-fast stain is less sensitive than the Gram stain; a negative modified stain does not exclude Nocardia. Lysozyme resistance separates Nocardia from Streptomyces.

cues.text: Nocardia is an aerobic actinomycete. On Gram stain it forms beaded, branching gram-positive filaments. With a modified acid-fast stain, using a weak acid decolouriser, it is partly acid-fast.
Colonies grow aerial filaments and usually appear in two to seven days, but slow strains need up to two or three weeks, so tell the lab to hold the culture.

It lives in soil and water and is inhaled or enters through the skin. In people with weak cellular immunity, such as transplant recipients or patients on steroids, it spreads from the lungs to the brain.
The modified acid-fast stain is less sensitive than the Gram stain, so a negative result does not rule Nocardia out. Lysozyme resistance separates it from Streptomyces.

props.label: Colonies 2–7 days · hold up to 2–3 weeks

scenes.title: Telling them apart, and what to report
scenes.altText: Comparison table: Listeria (short GPR, catalase +, motile at room temperature, not acid-fast) · Nocardia (beaded branching filaments, aerobic, partially acid-fast, aerial mycelia, lysozyme-resistant) · Actinomyces (branching gram-positive filaments too, but ANAEROBIC, part of normal oral/gut/genital flora, sulfur granules in tissue). Therapy notes (for context, not prescribing): Listeria — ampicillin or amoxicillin with gentamicin is the usual regimen, and most strains are intrinsically resistant to third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins; Nocardia — sulfa-containing drugs remain the drugs of choice, with susceptibility testing because species differ; Actinomyces — penicillin G or amoxicillin. Hook answers: (1) suspect Listeria; warn that cephalosporins alone do not cover it; (2) suspect Nocardia; request modified acid-fast stain and prolonged culture, and flag possible brain involvement.

cues.text: Compare three gram-positive rods. Listeria is short, catalase positive and motile at room temperature. Nocardia forms beaded, branching filaments and is aerobic and partly acid-fast.
Actinomyces also branches, but it is anaerobic, lives in the mouth, gut and genital tract, and forms sulfur granules in tissue.

Why it matters: Listeria is usually treated with ampicillin plus gentamicin, and most strains resist the cephalosporins often used for meningitis. Nocardia is treated with sulfa drugs, guided by susceptibility testing; Actinomyces with penicillin.

So, the newborn’s CSF suggests Listeria: tell the team cephalosporins alone will not cover it. The sputum suggests Nocardia: ask for a modified acid-fast stain and a long culture, and flag possible brain spread.

props.label: 1 → Listeria · 2 → Nocardia: modified AFB + long culture

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A third-generation cephalosporin covers neonatal Listeria meningitis” (✓ most strains are intrinsically resistant; ampicillin/amoxicillin ± gentamicin); “A negative modified acid-fast stain rules out Nocardia” (✓ the modified stain is less sensitive than the Gram stain); “Partially acid-fast branching rods in sputum = tuberculosis” (✓ nocardiosis can mimic tuberculosis clinically, but beaded branching filaments with aerial mycelia point to Nocardia; confirm by culture and identification).

cues.text: Trap one: a third-generation cephalosporin covers Listeria meningitis. No: most strains are naturally resistant; ampicillin with gentamicin is the usual choice.
Trap two: a negative modified acid-fast stain rules out Nocardia. No: it is less sensitive than the Gram stain.
Trap three: partly acid-fast branching rods in sputum mean tuberculosis. No: Nocardia can mimic tuberculosis, but beaded branching filaments with aerial growth point to Nocardia. Confirm by culture.

scenes.title: Fridge runner, soil climber
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “LISTERIA is the FRIDGE RUNNER: it grows in the cold, runs (is motile) at room temperature but stands still at body heat, and laughs at cephalosporins. NOCARDIA is the SOIL CLIMBER: it branches like a vine, holds a little acid stain, climbs from lung to brain, and is beaten with sulfa.” Tokens: fridge runner · soil climber · Actinomyces = anaerobic cousin. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Listeria is the fridge runner. It grows in the cold, runs at room temperature but stands still at body heat, and shrugs off cephalosporins. Nocardia is the soil climber. It branches like a vine, holds a little acid-fast stain, climbs from lung to brain, and is treated with sulfa drugs.
Where it breaks: Nocardia species differ in drug susceptibility, so testing guides therapy; the modified acid-fast stain can be negative; and Listeria can also infect healthy adults.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Listeria: GPR, catalase +, grows cold, motile ≤30 °C, neonates/pregnancy/immunocompromised, resists cephalosporins → ampicillin ± gentamicin”, “Nocardia: aerobic, beaded branching, partially acid-fast, soil → lung → brain, prolonged culture, sulfa · Actinomyces: anaerobic, sulfur granules”.

cues.text: Listeria is a cold-growing, catalase-positive rod that threatens newborns, pregnancy and the immunocompromised and is not covered by cephalosporins, while Nocardia is an aerobic, partially acid-fast branching soil organism that spreads from lung to brain and needs prolonged culture.

props.label: Nocardia: aerobic · partially acid-fast · lung → brain · hold culture

explanation.what: Plain language: Listeria is a small rod from contaminated chilled food that can grow even in the fridge and is dangerous for babies, pregnant women and people with weak immunity. Nocardia is a soil organism that grows as branching threads, can take weeks to grow in the lab, and can spread from the lungs to the brain in people with weak immunity. Scientific terms: gram-positive rod (GPR), catalase, psychrotrophic, flagellar motility (MogR/GmaR), rhombencephalitis, aerobic actinomycete, modified acid-fast stain, aerial mycelia, lysozyme resistance, sulfur granules.
explanation.why: Missing Listeria matters because common empirical cephalosporins do not cover it. Missing Nocardia matters because routine cultures may be discarded before it grows, and brain involvement changes management.
explanation.measure: Listeria: GPR, catalase +, grows about −0.4 to 45 °C, flagella expressed ≤30 °C and repressed at 37 °C; usual therapy ampicillin/amoxicillin with gentamicin; most strains intrinsically resistant to 3rd/4th-generation cephalosporins. Nocardia: beaded branching GP filaments, partially acid-fast with modified stain (less sensitive than Gram), colonies 2–7 days, slow strains 2–3 weeks; lysozyme resistance vs Streptomyces; shorter mycolic acids than mycobacteria; sulfa drugs of choice. Actinomyces: anaerobic, sulfur granules, penicillin.
explanation.differs: Listeria (short GPR, motile at room temperature) vs Nocardia (aerobic branching, partially acid-fast) vs Actinomyces (anaerobic branching, sulfur granules) vs mycobacteria (clinical mimic; Nocardia has shorter mycolic acids).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify Listeria from neonatal or pregnancy meningitis/sepsis with GPRs, recognise cephalosporin resistance, identify Nocardia from partially acid-fast branching rods in an immunocompromised host, and separate it from Actinomyces.

questions.stem: CSF from a 5-day-old neonate shows short gram-positive rods; the isolate is catalase-positive and motile at room temperature. Which empirical antibiotic would NOT cover this organism if used alone?

options.text: A third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime
options.rationale: Correct. Most Listeria strains are intrinsically resistant to third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins.
Incorrect. Ampicillin (with gentamicin) is the usual regimen.
Incorrect. Amoxicillin is an accepted alternative to ampicillin.
Incorrect. This is the usual combination.

questions.stem: Sputum from a transplant recipient on corticosteroids shows beaded, branching gram-positive filaments that are partially acid-fast with a modified stain. The isolate grows aerobically with aerial mycelia. What is the most likely organism?

options.rationale: Correct. Aerobic, branching, partially acid-fast filaments with aerial mycelia in an immunocompromised host.
Incorrect. Actinomyces branches but is anaerobic and forms sulfur granules.

Incorrect. Pulmonary nocardiosis can mimic tuberculosis clinically, but beaded branching filaments with aerial mycelia are characteristic of Nocardia, which differs from mycobacteria in having shorter mycolic acids.
Incorrect. Listeria is a short, non-branching rod and not acid-fast.

questions.stem: Nocardia is suspected, but the modified acid-fast stain on the sputum is negative. What should the laboratory do?

options.text: Rely on the Gram stain and hold cultures for up to 2–3 weeks
options.rationale: Correct. The modified stain is less sensitive than the Gram stain, and slow strains need prolonged incubation.
Incorrect. A negative modified stain does not exclude Nocardia.
Incorrect. Nocardia may take 2–7 days or longer to appear.
Incorrect. Nocardia is aerobic; anaerobic culture is for Actinomyces.
